\chapter{Hablaron --- They Spoke}
\label{ch:hablaron}
\hlchaptermodality{199}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what a group of people did, with -ar verbs in the past.}

I can say what a group of people did, with -ar verbs in the past.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hablaron]{hablaron}

\label{lesson:ES-C55-hablaron}



\begin{quote}
Give the three past forms you have. (\emph{Hablé, hablaste, habló}.) Now the present for \emph{they}. (\emph{Hablan}.)

You have had a past tense for one person only. Today it grows.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: they, in the past}]
\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{hablaron}} — they spoke
\end{quote}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{present} & \textbf{past} \\
\midrule
\emph{ellos / ellas / ustedes} & \textbf{hablan} & \textbf{hablaron} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The present ending is \emph{-an}. The past ending is \textbf{-aron}, and the stress lands on that \textbf{-a-}: \emph{ha-BLA-ron}. No written accent this time — the word already ends in \emph{-n}, and a word ending in \emph{-n} is stressed on the second-to-last syllable by default, which is exactly where the stress is.

So \emph{habló} needed its accent and \emph{hablaron} does not. The rule you learned for reading accents is doing the work.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{hablan · hablaron}
  \item \emph{trabajaron · estudiaron}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The past \emph{they} ending for \emph{-ar} verbs? (\textbf{-aron}.)

Does it take a written accent? (\textbf{No} — it ends in \emph{-n}, so the default stress is already correct.)
\end{tcolorbox}
